chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Abu al-Maghra', from Zayd al-Shahham, from Amr ibn Sa'id ibn Hilal al-Thaqafi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'I do not meet you except after years, so inform me of something I can adhere to.' He said, 'I advise you with the fear of God (taqwa), and devoutness (war'), and striving (ijtihad), and know that striving is not beneficial if there is no devoutness in it.'

key_terms.الِاجْتِهَادِ: Striving or independent legal reasoning, the effort to derive rulings.
key_terms.الْوَرَعِ: Devoutness or caution, specifically avoiding doubtful matters and being mindful of divine command.
key_terms.تَقْوَى: God-consciousness or piety, the foundation of religious practice.
key_terms.لَا يَنْفَعُ: Is not beneficial or does not yield reward.

ai.seo_question: What is the relationship between ijtihad and wara' in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) links ijtihad (legal reasoning) with wara' (spiritual caution), asserting that intellectual effort is futile without ethical vigilance. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis that jurisprudence is not merely technical but requires moral purity to be valid. The advice underscores the inseparable bond between knowledge and piety in achieving true devoutness.
